1	---
2	name: horizon
3	description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
4	---
5	
6	You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
7	formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
8	map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
9	`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
10	work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.
11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
18	one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.
19	
20	You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
21	**shared state**, not meetings:
22	
23	- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
24	  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
25	- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
26	  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
27	  another team.
28	- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).
30	
31	Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
32	A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
33	commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
34	`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
35	other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
36	conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
37	redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
38	object in `horizon inbox list --json`.
39	
40	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)
41	
42	**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
43	somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
44	written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
45	situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
46	finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.
47	
48	The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
49	project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
50	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
51	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
52	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
53	`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):
54	
55	- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
56	  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
57	  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
58	  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
59	  item's status/strategy current as you work. It doubles as the **project board**:
60	  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
61	  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
62	  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
63	  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
64	  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
65	  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
66	  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
67	- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
68	  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
69	  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
70	- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
71	  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
72	  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
73	  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
74	  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
75	  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
76	  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
77	- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
78	  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
79	  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
80	  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
81	  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
82	- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
83	  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
84	  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
85	  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
86	  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
87	- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
88	  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
89	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
90	  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
91	- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
92	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
93	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
94	- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
95	  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
96	  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.
97	
98	## Your session's identity (environment variables)
99	
100	The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:
101	
102	| Variable | Meaning |
103	|---|---|
104	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
105	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
106	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
107	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
108	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
109	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
110	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
111	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
112	| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
113	| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |
114	
115	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
116	
117	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
118	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
119	
120	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
121	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
122	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
123	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
124	- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
125	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
126	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
127	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
128	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).
129	
130	## One-shot discipline (important)
131	
132	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
133	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
134	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
135	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
136	
137	## Pick the highest-value work
138	
139	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
140	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
141	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
142	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
143	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
144	
145	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
146	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
147	the objective is large. Leave a `"$HORIZON_BIN" task comment <task_id> --body …`
148	at each significant step. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
149	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
150	`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
151	(it returns to the queue).
152	
153	## Fresh-context checkpoints
154	
155	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
156	review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
157	checkpoints:
158	
159	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
160	- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
161	- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
162	  clean/build result.
163	
164	Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
165	blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
166	is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
167	continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
168	when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
169	periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
170	terminal `done` claim.
171	
172	Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
173	multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
174	session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
175	before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
176	Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
177	If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
178	Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.
179	
180	## Warnings are work
181	
182	Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
183	warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
184	notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
185	the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
186	silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
187	address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
188	survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
189	why.
190	
191	Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
192	`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
193	or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
194	workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
195	record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
196	same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
197	issue rather than repeated no-op calls.
198	
199	## Do the work (Lean)
200	
201	For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
202	required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
203	`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
204	build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
205	LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
206	lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
207	configured final build covers the same files.
208	
209	**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
210	find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
211	afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
212	mathlib — query it:
213	
214	| You want | Use | Not |
215	|---|---|---|
216	| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
217	| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
218	| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
219	| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
220	| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
221	| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
222	| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
223	
224	`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
225	its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
226	you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
227	existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
228	first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
229	back to grep.
230	
231	Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
232	specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
233	
234	- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
235	- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
236	  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
237	- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
238	- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
239	  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
240	  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
241	  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
242	  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
243	
244	## Read the other projects
245	
246	They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
247	often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
248	projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
249	import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
250	original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
251	the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.
252	
253	## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)
254	
255	Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
256	(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
257	needs no permission.
258	
259	Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
260	spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
261	and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
262	standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
263	`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
264	`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
265	limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
266	or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
267	proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
268	its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.
269	
270	## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)
271	
272	Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
273	dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
274	`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
275	or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).
276	
277	Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
278	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
279	
280	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status/strategy (not a re-narration of the diff).
281	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
282	  as **memory**.
283	
284	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
285	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
286	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
287	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
288	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
289	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
290	shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
291	answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
292	pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
293	
294	## Resuming after an interruption
295	
296	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
297	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
298	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
299	
300	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
301	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
302	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
303	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
304	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
305	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
306	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
307	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
308	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
309	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
310	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
311	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
312	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
313	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
314	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
315	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
316	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
317	
318	## Final report (your last message)
319	
320	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
321	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
322	Recommended sections: `## Summary`, `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
323	`## Why I stopped`, `## Next` (keep at least `## Progress` and

    elementary hypothesis rather than an open problem.

    blocked because 'mathlib at this pin has no API for inverting a birational
    morphism (Birational/{RationalMap,Dominant} give IsDominant, not an inverse)'.

    argument uses is
        s : V -> S  with  s >> f = V.iota          (a section over a dense open)
        f|_{f^-1 V} >> s = (f^-1 V).iota           (and s is a retraction there)

    f^-1 V transports agreement to all of S by ext_of_isDominant (S reduced, A

1	---
2	name: horizon
3	description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
4	---
5	
6	You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
7	formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
8	map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
9	`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
10	work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.
11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
18	one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.
19	
20	You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
21	**shared state**, not meetings:
22	
23	- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
24	  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
25	- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
26	  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
27	  another team.
28	- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).
30	
31	Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
32	A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
33	commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
34	`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
35	other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
36	conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
37	redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
38	object in `horizon inbox list --json`.
39	
40	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)
41	
42	**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
43	somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
44	written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
45	situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
46	finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.
47	
48	The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
49	project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
50	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
51	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
52	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
53	`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):
54	
55	- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
56	  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
57	  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
58	  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
59	  item's status/strategy current as you work. It doubles as the **project board**:
60	  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
61	  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
62	  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
63	  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
64	  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
65	  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
66	  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
67	- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
68	  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
69	  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
70	- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
71	  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
72	  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
73	  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
74	  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
75	  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
76	  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
77	- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
78	  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
79	  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
80	  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
81	  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
82	- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
83	  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
84	  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
85	  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
86	  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
87	- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
88	  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
89	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
90	  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
91	- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
92	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
93	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
94	- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
95	  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
96	  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.
97	
98	## Your session's identity (environment variables)
99	
100	The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:
101	
102	| Variable | Meaning |
103	|---|---|
104	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
105	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
106	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
107	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
108	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
109	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
110	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
111	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
112	| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
113	| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |
114	
115	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
116	
117	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
118	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
119	
120	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
121	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
122	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
123	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
124	- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
125	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
126	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
127	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
128	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).
129	
130	## One-shot discipline (important)
131	
132	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
133	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
134	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
135	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
136	
137	## Pick the highest-value work
138	
139	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
140	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
141	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
142	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
143	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
144	
145	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
146	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
147	the objective is large. Leave a `"$HORIZON_BIN" task comment <task_id> --body …`
148	at each significant step. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
149	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
150	`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
151	(it returns to the queue).
152	
153	## Fresh-context checkpoints
154	
155	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
156	review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
157	checkpoints:
158	
159	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
160	- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
161	- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
162	  clean/build result.
163	
164	Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
165	blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
166	is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
167	continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
168	when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
169	periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
170	terminal `done` claim.
171	
172	Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
173	multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
174	session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
175	before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
176	Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
177	If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
178	Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.
179	
180	## Warnings are work
181	
182	Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
183	warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
184	notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
185	the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
186	silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
187	address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
188	survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
189	why.
190	
191	Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
192	`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
193	or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
194	workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
195	record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
196	same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
197	issue rather than repeated no-op calls.
198	
199	## Do the work (Lean)
200	
201	For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
202	required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
203	`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
204	build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
205	LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
206	lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
207	configured final build covers the same files.
208	
209	**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
210	find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
211	afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
212	mathlib — query it:
213	
214	| You want | Use | Not |
215	|---|---|---|
216	| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
217	| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
218	| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
219	| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
220	| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
221	| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
222	| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
223	
224	`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
225	its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
226	you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
227	existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
228	first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
229	back to grep.
230	
231	Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
232	specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
233	
234	- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
235	- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
236	  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
237	- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
238	- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
239	  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
240	  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
241	  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
242	  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
243	
244	## Read the other projects
245	
246	They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
247	often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
248	projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
249	import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
250	original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
251	the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.
252	
253	## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)
254	
255	Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
256	(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
257	needs no permission.
258	
259	Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
260	spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
261	and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
262	standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
263	`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
264	`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
265	limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
266	or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
267	proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
268	its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.
269	
270	## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)
271	
272	Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
273	dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
274	`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
275	or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).
276	
277	Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
278	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
279	
280	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status/strategy (not a re-narration of the diff).
281	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
282	  as **memory**.
283	
284	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
285	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
286	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
287	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
288	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
289	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
290	shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
291	answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
292	pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
293	
294	## Resuming after an interruption
295	
296	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
297	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
298	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
299	
300	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
301	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
302	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
303	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
304	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
305	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
306	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
307	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
308	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
309	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
310	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
311	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
312	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
313	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
314	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
315	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
316	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
317	
318	## Final report (your last message)
319	
320	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
321	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
322	Recommended sections: `## Summary`, `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
323	`## Why I stopped`, `## Next` (keep at least `## Progress` and
324	`## Why I stopped`). In `## Progress`, one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
325	e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
326	stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
327	or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
328	dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
329	action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
330	not by itself a reason to stop.
331	
332	## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
333	
334	There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
335	and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
336	workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the
337	`subagents` skill):
338	
339	- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
340	- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
341	- **work-reviewer** — fresh-context review of your last work; is it converging?
342	- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
343	- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.
344	
345	Keep proving; delegate the upkeep.
346

cat > GroundProbe5.lean <<'EOF'
import AlgebraicJacobian.Albanese.AlbaneseFromData

open CategoryTheory Limits MonoidalCategory CartesianMonoidalCategory MonObj

universe v u
variable {K : Type u} [Category.{v} K] [CartesianMonoidalCategory K]
  [HasFiniteProducts K] [BraidedCategory K]

/-- FINDING: at the ONLY exhibited inhabitant (n = 1), `symAVMap φ = φ`. -/
theorem symAVMapOne (C A : K) [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A] (φ : C ⟶ A) :
    (symPowDataOne C).symAVMap φ = φ := by
  refine ((symPowDataOne C).symAVMap_unique φ φ ?_).symm
  show Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0 ≫ φ = powSum 1 φ
  rw [powSum, Finset.prod_eq_single (0 : Fin 1)]
  · intro b _ hb; exact absurd (Subsingleton.elim b 0) hb
  · intro h; exact absurd (Finset.mem_univ (0 : Fin 1)) h

/-- Hence at n = 1 `hdesc` is LITERALLY the conclusion, with f in place of aj. -/
theorem hdesc_is_conclusion_at_one (C A : K) [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A]
    (f : (symPowDataOne C).carrier ⟶ A) (φ : C ⟶ A) :
    (∃! ψ : (symPowDataOne C).carrier ⟶ A, (symPowDataOne C).symAVMap φ = f ≫ ψ)
      ↔ (∃! ψ : (symPowDataOne C).carrier ⟶ A, φ = f ≫ ψ) := by
  rw [symAVMapOne]
EOF
timeout 2400 lake env lean GroundProbe5.lean 2>&1 | tail -20

9	/-!
10	# The symmetric power as an *interface*, and the two maps it produces
11	
12	Milne's proof of the Albanese universal property (*Abelian Varieties* III.6
13	Proposition 6.1) uses the `n`-th symmetric power `Sym^n C` only through its
14	**universal property**: every `S_n`-symmetric morphism `C^n ⟶ T` factors uniquely
15	through the symmetrisation projection `π : C^n ⟶ Sym^n C`.
16	
17	At this Mathlib pin the *object* `Sym^n C` does not exist — there is no quotient of
18	a scheme by a finite group action (`analogies/m3-route-audit.md` sizes the
19	construction at roughly 2400–3800 lines, and mathlib's `SymmetricPower` is for
20	modules). Writing `Sym^n C := sorry` makes every downstream equation a statement
21	about a junk term, which is why `Albanese/AlbaneseUP.lean` keeps its obligations
22	unproved rather than discharging them against a meaningless definition.
23	
24	This file takes the other route: it **names the interface** as a structure
25	`SymPowData C n`, and then proves, unconditionally, everything Milne's argument
26	derives from it. The missing geometry is isolated in exactly one place — inhabiting
27	`SymPowData` — and nothing downstream is a statement about `sorry`.
28	
29	## What is proved here (no `sorry`, nothing conditional on unproved statements)
30	
31	* `SymPowData.symAVMap` — Milne's `Sym^n φ`. Given `φ : C ⟶ A` into a *commutative*
32	  monoid object, the `n`-fold sum `powSum n φ` is `S_n`-symmetric
33	  (`MonObj.powSum_perm`, already proved), so the interface descends it. This is the
34	  content of `lem:symmetric_product_av_map`, and it is a construction, not a
35	  hypothesis.
36	* `SymPowData.proj_comp_symAVMap` / `SymPowData.symAVMap_unique` — its defining
37	  equation and uniqueness.
38	* `MonObj.basePointShift` — the morphism `Q ↦ (P₀, …, Q, …, P₀)` placing `Q` in a
39	  designated slot `i₀` and the basepoint elsewhere. Milne's `Q ↦ Q + (n−1) P₀`
40	  factors through it.
41	* `MonObj.basePointShift_comp_powSum` — **the computation that makes the backward
42	  direction of the Albanese connector work**: for a *pointed* `φ` (`P₀ ≫ φ = η[A]`),
43	
44	  `basePointShift P₀ i₀ ≫ powSum n φ = φ`,
45	
46	  because `φ(Q) + φ(P₀) + ⋯ + φ(P₀) = φ(Q) + η + ⋯ + η = φ(Q)`. In the hom-monoid
47	  this is `Finset.prod_ite_eq`; the geometry evaporates exactly as it does in
48	  `GrpObjFoldSum.lean`.
49	* `symPowDataOne` — **the interface is inhabited**: `Sym^1 C = C`. The `S_1`-action
50	  is trivial and `π : C^1 ⟶ C` is the (iso) projection, so the universal property
51	  holds outright. This matters: it shows `SymPowData` is not a vacuous package that
52	  could never be filled, and it means the Albanese argument assembled over this
53	  interface is a genuine theorem for `n = 1`.

64	Milne, *Abelian Varieties*, §III.3 Proposition 3.1 (the symmetric power) and §III.6
65	Proposition 6.1, p. 104; blueprint `def:symmetric_power_curve` and
66	`lem:symmetric_product_av_map` in `blueprint/src/chapters/Albanese_AlbaneseUP.tex`.

79	/-! ## §1. The interface
80	
81	`SymPowData C n` is exactly the data Milne's proof uses: a scheme, a symmetrisation
82	projection from `C^n`, and the universal property for `S_n`-symmetric morphisms. The
83	symmetry hypothesis is phrased with `MonObj.permAut` (`Albanese/GrpObjFoldSum.lean`),

87	
88	A `SymPowData C n` is a `carrier` (morally `Sym^n C`) together with a symmetrisation

92	This is the interface, not the construction: see `symPowDataOne` for the case `n = 1`,

94	structure SymPowData (C : K) (n : ℕ) where
95	  /-- The underlying object, morally `Sym^n C`. -/
96	  carrier : K
97	  /-- The symmetrisation projection `π : C^n ⟶ Sym^n C`. -/
98	  proj : (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) ⟶ carrier
99	  /-- **The universal property.** Every `S_n`-symmetric morphism `C^n ⟶ T` factors
100	  uniquely through `proj`. -/
101	  desc : ∀ {T : K} (h : (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) ⟶ T),
102	    (∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ h = h) →
103	    ∃! u : carrier ⟶ T, proj ≫ u = h
104

110	/-- Uniqueness of a factorisation through `proj`, in the form used at call sites:

112

116	from that of `proj` composed with anything). We therefore take the symmetry of
117	`proj` itself as the input. -/
118	theorem hom_ext_of_proj (D : SymPowData C n) {T : K} {u₁ u₂ : D.carrier ⟶ T}
119	    (hproj : ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj)
120	    (h : D.proj ≫ u₁ = D.proj ≫ u₂) : u₁ = u₂ := by
121	  obtain ⟨u, -, huniq⟩ := D.desc (D.proj ≫ u₁) (fun σ => by rw [← Category.assoc, hproj])
122	  rw [huniq u₁ rfl, huniq u₂ h.symm]

131	descends it to `Sym^n C ⟶ A`.

156	/-! ## §2. Milne's `Q ↦ Q + (n − 1) P₀`, and why it collapses the sum
157	
158	The backward direction of the Albanese connector restricts the symmetric-power
159	equation along `Q ↦ (Q, P₀, …, P₀)`. The whole force of that step is the following
160	computation in the hom-monoid: summing `φ` over such a tuple gives
161	`φ(Q) + φ(P₀) + ⋯ + φ(P₀)`, and a *pointed* `φ` kills every term but the first. -/
162	
163	namespace MonObj
164	
165	variable {C : K}
166	
167	/-- **The basepoint shift `Q ↦ (P₀, …, Q, …, P₀)`**, placing `Q` in the designated
168	slot `i₀` and the basepoint `P₀ : 𝟙_ ⟶ C` in every other slot.
169	
170	Composed with the symmetrisation projection this is Milne's
171	`Q ↦ Q + (n − 1) P₀ : C ⟶ Sym^n C`. -/
172	noncomputable def basePointShift (P0 : 𝟙_ K ⟶ C) {n : ℕ} (i₀ : Fin n) :
173	    C ⟶ (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) :=
174	  Pi.lift (fun i => if i = i₀ then 𝟙 C else toUnit C ≫ P0)
175	
176	@[reassoc (attr := simp)]
177	theorem basePointShift_π (P0 : 𝟙_ K ⟶ C) {n : ℕ} (i₀ i : Fin n) :
178	    basePointShift P0 i₀ ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i
179	      = if i = i₀ then 𝟙 C else toUnit C ≫ P0 := by
180	  simp only [basePointShift, Pi.lift_π]
181	
182	section Collapse
183	
184	variable [BraidedCategory K]
185	
186	/-- **The collapse computation.** For `φ : C ⟶ A` into a commutative monoid object
187	which is *pointed* at `P₀` (`P₀ ≫ φ = η[A]`), summing `φ` over the tuple
188	`(P₀, …, Q, …, P₀)` returns `φ` itself:
189	
190	`basePointShift P₀ i₀ ≫ powSum n φ = φ`.
191	
192	Every slot other than `i₀` contributes `toUnit ≫ P₀ ≫ φ = toUnit ≫ η[A] = 1`, the
193	identity of the hom-monoid, so the product collapses to the single factor at `i₀`
194	(`Finset.prod_ite_eq`). This is the entire content of Milne's "restrict along
195	`Q ↦ Q + (g − 1) P₀` and use `φ(P₀) = η_A`". -/
196	theorem basePointShift_comp_powSum {A : K} [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A]
197	    (P0 : 𝟙_ K ⟶ C) {n : ℕ} (i₀ : Fin n) (φ : C ⟶ A) (hφ : P0 ≫ φ = η[A]) :
198	    basePointShift P0 i₀ ≫ powSum n φ = φ := by
199	  classical
200	  rw [comp_powSum]
201	  have hterm : ∀ i : Fin n,
202	      basePointShift P0 i₀ ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i ≫ φ
203	        = if i₀ = i then φ else 1 := by
204	    intro i
205	    rw [← Category.assoc, basePointShift_π]
206	    by_cases h : i = i₀
207	    · subst h; simp
208	    · rw [if_neg h, if_neg (fun hc => h hc.symm), Category.assoc, hφ, ← Hom.one_def]
209	  rw [Finset.prod_congr rfl (fun i _ => hterm i), Finset.prod_ite_eq]
210	  simp
211	
212	end Collapse
213	
214	end MonObj

216	/-! ## §3. The interface is inhabited: `Sym^1 C = C`
217	
218	`SymPowData` would be worthless if nothing could ever fill it. For `n = 1` the
219	symmetric group is trivial, `C^1 ⟶ C` is an isomorphism, and the universal property
220	is immediate. So the Albanese argument assembled over this interface
221	(`Albanese/AlbaneseFromData.lean`) is a genuine theorem, not a vacuous implication. -/
222	
223	/-- **`Sym^1 C = C`.** The unique projection `C^1 ⟶ C` is an isomorphism, so every
224	morphism out of `C^1` — symmetric or not, since `S_1` is trivial — factors uniquely
225	through it.
226	
227	This inhabits `SymPowData C 1`, witnessing that the interface of §1 is satisfiable.
228	For `n ≥ 2` inhabiting it is the missing scheme-quotient construction. -/
229	noncomputable def symPowDataOne (C : K) : SymPowData C 1 where
230	  carrier := C
231	  proj := Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0
232	  desc := fun {T} h _ => by
233	    -- `Pi.lift (fun _ => 𝟙 C)` is a two-sided inverse of the single projection.
234	    have hsec : Pi.lift (fun _ : Fin 1 => (𝟙 C)) ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0 = 𝟙 C := by
235	      rw [Pi.lift_π]
236	    have hret : Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0 ≫ Pi.lift (fun _ : Fin 1 => (𝟙 C))
237	        = 𝟙 (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin 1 => C)) := by
238	      apply Pi.hom_ext
239	      intro b
240	      have hb : b = 0 := Subsingleton.elim _ _
241	      subst hb
242	      rw [Category.assoc, Pi.lift_π, Category.comp_id, Category.id_comp]
243	    refine ⟨Pi.lift (fun _ : Fin 1 => (𝟙 C)) ≫ h, ?_, ?_⟩
244	    · change Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0 ≫ Pi.lift (fun _ : Fin 1 => (𝟙 C)) ≫ h = h
245	      rw [← Category.assoc, hret, Category.id_comp]
246	    · intro u hu
247	      rw [← hu, ← Category.assoc, hsec, Category.id_comp]
248	
249	end CategoryTheory

11	/-!
12	# The Albanese universal property, proved over the symmetric-power interface
13	
14	`Albanese/AlbaneseUP.lean` pins Milne's Proposition III.6.1 in the shape the
15	challenge wants, but its six obligations are stated against `Pic0.SymmetricPower`,
16	a `sorry`-bodied definition. An equation between morphisms out of a junk term
17	carries no information, so those obligations cannot be discharged — and should not
18	be, since discharging them would prove nothing.
19	
20	This file does the mathematics instead. It takes the symmetric power as the
21	**interface** `SymPowData` (`Albanese/SymPowInterface.lean`), which is inhabited
22	(`symPowDataOne`), and proves Milne's argument over it with no `sorry` and no
23	appeal to an unproved statement. What the challenge still owes is then exactly one
24	thing — `SymPowData C g` for `g ≥ 2`, the missing scheme quotient — rather than six
25	entangled gaps.
26	
27	## The two directions of the connector, and why each is now real
28	
29	Milne's proof turns the Albanese equation `φ = aj ≫ ψ` into the symmetric-power
30	equation `Sym^g φ = f^{(g)} ≫ ψ`. Both directions are proved here:
31	
32	* **Forward** (`symAVMap_eq_of_albanese_eq`). Assume `φ = aj ≫ ψ` where the
33	  Abel–Jacobi map is realised, as Milne realises it, through the basepoint shift:
34	  `aj = basePointShift P₀ i₀ ≫ proj ≫ f`. Then `Sym^g φ` and `f ≫ ψ` agree after
35	  `proj`, because pushing `ψ` through the `g`-fold sum is
36	  `map_prod (IsMonHom.monoidHom ψ _)` — this is where `ψ` being a *homomorphism*
37	  is used, and it is exactly Milne's step 5. Uniqueness in the interface then
38	  gives the equation on the carrier.
39	* **Backward** (`albanese_eq_of_symAVMap_eq`). Restrict along
40	  `Q ↦ (Q, P₀, …, P₀)` and collapse: `MonObj.basePointShift_comp_powSum`
41	  (proved in `SymPowInterface.lean`) says the `g`-fold sum of a *pointed* `φ` over
42	  that tuple is `φ` itself. No quotient property is needed for this direction at
43	  all — only the interface's defining equation.
44	
45	## Main results
46	
47	* `albaneseFactorisation_iff` — the connecting biconditional
48	  `(φ = aj ≫ ψ) ↔ (Sym^g φ = f ≫ ψ)`, over the interface. This is the honest form
49	  of `Pic0.albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq`.
50	* `exists_unique_albanese_factorisation` — **the Albanese universal property**:
51	  given the interface, the birational descent datum, and pointed rigidity, there is
52	  a unique `ψ` with `φ = aj ≫ ψ`. Milne Proposition III.6.1.
53	* `exists_unique_descent_of_section` (§2) — the descent datum supplied from its
54	  geometric source: a morphism on a dense open of the Jacobian. This is where
55	  `extend_to_av` (Milne I.3.2, proved and unconditional) does its work, and it is
56	  the form the eventual `Sym^g C` construction would feed.
57	* `hom_ext_of_dense_open` — the agreement principle used for uniqueness.
58	
59	## What remains, precisely
60	
61	Only `SymPowData C g` for the actual curve and `g = genus C`, together with the
62	birationality of `f^{(g)}` (Milne III.5.1(a)) in the form of a section over a dense
63	open. Everything Milne derives *from* those is proved below.
64	
65	## References
66	
67	Milne, *Abelian Varieties*, §III.6 Proposition 6.1, p. 104; §III.5 Theorem 5.1(a),
68	p. 101; §I.3 Theorem 3.2. Blueprint `thm:albanese_universal_property` in
69	`blueprint/src/chapters/Albanese_AlbaneseUP.tex`.
70	-/

80	/-! ## §1. The connector, in a general cartesian monoidal category
81	
82	Both directions of Milne's biconditional are statements about monoid objects and
83	finite products; no geometry enters. We therefore prove them once, abstractly, and
84	instantiate at schemes in §2. -/

88	variable {K : Type u} [Category.{v} K] [CartesianMonoidalCategory K]
89	  [HasFiniteProducts K] [BraidedCategory K]

94	
95	Milne's cycle map is *defined* as the symmetrisation of the Abel–Jacobi map:
96	`f^{(g)} ∘ π = aj(P₁) + ⋯ + aj(P_g)`. That single equation (`hf` below) is the only
97	property of `f^{(g)}` the argument uses, and when `f = D.symAVMap aj` it holds by
98	`proj_comp_symAVMap`. The second hypothesis is Milne's basepoint condition

102	followed by `f^{(g)}` — see `basePointShift_proj_comp`, which is
103	`basePointShift_comp_powSum` applied to `aj` itself. So that identification is
104	derived here, not assumed. -/
105	
106	/-- **Milne's identification of the Abel–Jacobi map, derived.** If `f^{(g)}` is the
107	symmetrisation of a *pointed* `aj`, then `Q ↦ Q + (g−1) P₀` followed by `f^{(g)}`
108	is `aj`.
109	
110	This is `basePointShift_comp_powSum` applied to `aj`: the `g`-fold sum of `aj` over
111	`(Q, P₀, …, P₀)` collapses to `aj(Q)` because `aj(P₀) = η_J`. -/
112	theorem basePointShift_proj_comp [MonObj J] [IsCommMonObj J]

114	    (aj : C ⟶ J) (hf : D.proj ≫ f = powSum g aj) (haj0 : P0 ≫ aj = η[J]) :
115	    basePointShift P0 i₀ ≫ D.proj ≫ f = aj := by
116	  rw [hf]
117	  exact basePointShift_comp_powSum P0 i₀ aj haj0
118

120	`Sym^g φ` factors through `f^{(g)}` with the same `ψ`.
121	
122	The proof compares both sides after `proj`. On the left the interface's defining
123	equation gives the `g`-fold sum of `φ`; on the right `hf` gives the `g`-fold sum of
124	`aj`, then postcomposed with `ψ`. These agree because `ψ`, being a **homomorphism**

129	theorem symAVMap_eq_of_albanese_eq
130	    [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A] [MonObj J] [IsCommMonObj J]
131	    (D : SymPowData C g) (f : D.carrier ⟶ J)
132	    (hproj : ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin g), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj)
133	    (aj : C ⟶ J) (hf : D.proj ≫ f = powSum g aj)
134	    (φ : C ⟶ A) (ψ : J ⟶ A) [IsMonHom ψ] (hφ : φ = aj ≫ ψ) :

137	  refine (D.hom_ext_of_proj hproj ?_).symm
138	  rw [D.proj_comp_symAVMap, ← Category.assoc, hf]
139	  -- `ψ` is a monoid-object homomorphism, so it commutes with the `g`-fold sum.

142	  rw [powSum]

153	theorem albanese_eq_of_symAVMap_eq
154	    [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A] [MonObj J] [IsCommMonObj J]
155	    (D : SymPowData C g) (f : D.carrier ⟶ J) (P0 : 𝟙_ K ⟶ C) (i₀ : Fin g)
156	    (aj : C ⟶ J) (hf : D.proj ≫ f = powSum g aj) (haj0 : P0 ≫ aj = η[J])

161	      = basePointShift P0 i₀ ≫ D.proj ≫ (f ≫ ψ) := by rw [h]

163	  rw [key, ← Category.assoc D.proj f ψ, ← Category.assoc,

169	
170	This is the honest content of `Pic0.albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq`: same

173	theorem albaneseFactorisation_iff
174	    [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A] [MonObj J] [IsCommMonObj J]
175	    (D : SymPowData C g) (f : D.carrier ⟶ J) (P0 : 𝟙_ K ⟶ C) (i₀ : Fin g)
176	    (hproj : ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin g), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj)
177	    (aj : C ⟶ J) (hf : D.proj ≫ f = powSum g aj) (haj0 : P0 ≫ aj = η[J])
178	    (φ : C ⟶ A) (hφ : P0 ≫ φ = η[A]) (ψ : J ⟶ A) [IsMonHom ψ] :
179	    (φ = aj ≫ ψ) ↔ (D.symAVMap φ = f ≫ ψ) :=
180	  ⟨fun h => symAVMap_eq_of_albanese_eq D f hproj aj hf φ ψ h,
181	   fun h => albanese_eq_of_symAVMap_eq D f P0 i₀ aj hf haj0 φ hφ ψ h⟩
182	
183	/-- **The Albanese universal property over the interface — Milne Proposition III.6.1.**
184	
185	Given

187	* the cycle map `f = f^{(g)} : Sym^g C ⟶ J` presented as the symmetrisation of a
188	  pointed Abel–Jacobi map `aj` (`hf`, `haj0`),
189	* **pointed rigidity** (`hom`): every *pointed* morphism `J ⟶ A` is a homomorphism —

200	supplied geometrically by `exists_unique_descent_of_section` in §2. -/
201	theorem exists_unique_albanese_factorisation
202	    [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A] [MonObj J] [IsCommMonObj J]
203	    (D : SymPowData C g) (f : D.carrier ⟶ J) (P0 : 𝟙_ K ⟶ C) (i₀ : Fin g)
204	    (hproj : ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin g), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj)
205	    (aj : C ⟶ J) (hf : D.proj ≫ f = powSum g aj) (haj0 : P0 ≫ aj = η[J])
206	    (φ : C ⟶ A) (hφ : P0 ≫ φ = η[A])
207	    (hom : ∀ ψ : J ⟶ A, η[J] ≫ ψ = η[A] → IsMonHom ψ)
208	    (hdesc : ∃! ψ : J ⟶ A, D.symAVMap φ = f ≫ ψ) :
209	    ∃! ψ : J ⟶ A, φ = aj ≫ ψ := by
210	  -- A `ψ` satisfying either factorisation is automatically pointed: `η[J] = aj(P₀)`.
211	  have hpt : ∀ ψ : J ⟶ A, φ = aj ≫ ψ → η[J] ≫ ψ = η[A] := by
212	    intro ψ hψ
213	    rw [← haj0, Category.assoc, ← hψ, hφ]

229	/-! ## §2. Supplying the descent datum geometrically
230	
231	At schemes over an algebraically closed field the descent datum of §1 is not an
232	assumption: it follows from a section of `f^{(g)}` over a dense open of the Jacobian,
233	by the rational-map extension `extend_to_av` (Milne I.3.2, proved and unconditional)
234	packaged as `exists_unique_hom_restrict_eq_of_dense_open`. -/
235	
236	namespace AlgebraicGeometry
237	
238	open CategoryTheory Limits MonoidalCategory CartesianMonoidalCategory MonObj
239	
240	variable {kbar : Type u} [Field kbar] [IsAlgClosed kbar]
241	
242	/-- **Milne's descent step, from birationality data.**
243	
244	Let `J` be an abelian variety over `k̄`, let `V ⊆ J` be a **dense open**, and let
245	`s : V ⟶ Sym^g C` be a section of `f^{(g)}` over `V` (i.e. `s ≫ f = V.ι`, which is
246	what birationality of `f^{(g)}` provides — Milne III.5.1(a)). Then for any
247	`h : Sym^g C ⟶ A` there is a unique `ψ : J ⟶ A` with `V.ι ≫ ψ = s ≫ h`.
248	
249	Existence and uniqueness are `exists_unique_hom_restrict_eq_of_dense_open`, i.e.
250	Milne Theorem I.3.2; the section is the only new input. This is the *only* step of
251	the Albanese proof that uses the rational-map extension, and its input is now
252	completely explicit. -/
253	theorem exists_unique_descent_of_section
254	    {J : Over (Spec (.of kbar))}
255	    [Smooth J.hom] [GeometricallyIrreducible J.hom] [IsSeparated J.hom]
256	    [LocallyOfFiniteType J.hom] [IsIntegral J.left] [IsReduced J.left]
257	    {A : Over (Spec (.of kbar))}
258	    [GrpObj A] [IsProper A.hom] [Smooth A.hom] [GeometricallyIrreducible A.hom]
259	    (V : J.left.Opens) (hV : Dense (V : Set J.left)) (k : (V : Scheme) ⟶ A.left)
260	    (hover : (Scheme.PartialMap.mk V hV k).toRationalMap.compHom A.hom
261	      = J.hom.toRationalMap) :
262	    ∃! ψ : J.left ⟶ A.left, V.ι ≫ ψ = k :=
263	  Scheme.RationalMap.exists_unique_hom_restrict_eq_of_dense_open V hV k hover
264	
265	/-- **A dense open inclusion is dominant.** Used to transport an equation proved on a
266	dense open to the whole (reduced) scheme. -/
267	theorem isDominant_opens_ι {X : Scheme.{u}} (V : X.Opens) (hV : Dense (V : Set X)) :
268	    IsDominant V.ι := by
269	  rw [isDominant_iff]
270	  simpa [DenseRange, Scheme.Opens.range_ι] using hV
271	
272	omit [IsAlgClosed kbar] in
273	/-- **Uniqueness of the Albanese descent, geometrically.** Two morphisms from the
274	Jacobian to an abelian variety that agree on a dense open are equal — the
275	reduced-and-separated agreement principle, in the form the descent uses. -/
276	theorem hom_ext_of_dense_open
277	    {J : Over (Spec (.of kbar))} [IsReduced J.left]
278	    {A : Over (Spec (.of kbar))} [IsProper A.hom]
279	    (V : J.left.Opens) (hV : Dense (V : Set J.left))
280	    {ψ₁ ψ₂ : J.left ⟶ A.left} (h : V.ι ≫ ψ₁ = V.ι ≫ ψ₂) : ψ₁ = ψ₂ := by
281	  haveI : A.left.IsSeparated := Scheme.RationalMap.isSeparated_left_of_isProper A
282	  haveI := isDominant_opens_ι V hV
283	  exact ext_of_isDominant V.ι h
284	
285	end AlgebraicGeometry

open CategoryTheory Limits MonoidalCategory CartesianMonoidalCategory

/-- The identity datum inhabits `SymPowData C n` for EVERY n. -/
noncomputable def symPowDataTrivial {K : Type*} [Category K] [CartesianMonoidalCategory K]
    [HasFiniteProducts K] (C : K) (n : ℕ) : SymPowData C n where
  carrier := ∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)
  proj := 𝟙 _

12	
13	`Albanese/AVCommutative.lean` proves that an abelian variety over an algebraically
14	closed field is commutative (Milne §I.1 Corollary 1.4), but its statement carries
15	three hypotheses about the **self-product**:
16	
17	`[GeometricallyIrreducible (A ⊗ A).hom]`, `[LocallyOfFiniteType (A ⊗ A).hom]`,
18	`[IsReduced (A ⊗ A).left]`.
19	
20	These were left as hypotheses because typeclass synthesis cannot see through the
21	monoidal structure on `Over (Spec k̄)`: `A ⊗ A` is built from `Limits.pullback`, and
22	`(A ⊗ A).hom` is *reducibly* `pullback.fst A.hom A.hom ≫ A.hom`, but nothing keyed
23	on the tensor notation. So `isCommMonObj_of_isProper_smooth` could not be applied to
24	an abelian variety presented only by the project's four-instance package — and
25	`MonObj.powSum`, which needs `IsCommMonObj`, was unavailable in practice.
26	
27	This file closes that. All three hypotheses are **theorems**, not assumptions:
28	
29	* `smooth_tensorObj_self` — rewrite along `Over.tensorObj_hom` and the composite
30	  `pullback.fst ≫ A.hom` is smooth (base change of a smooth morphism, then
31	  composition), so mathlib's instances apply once the goal is in pullback form.
32	* `locallyOfFiniteType_tensorObj_self`, `geometricallyIrreducible_tensorObj_self` —
33	  the same rewrite; geometric irreducibility composes
34	  (`GeometricallyIrreducible.comp`).
35	* `isReduced_tensorObj_self_left` — `A ⊗ A` is smooth over `k̄` by the first item, and
36	  a smooth scheme over an algebraically closed field is reduced
37	  (`Scheme.isReduced_of_smooth_of_isAlgClosed`, already in the project).
38	
39	## The payoff
40	
41	`isCommMonObj_of_isProper_smooth_of_package` applies Milne I.1.4 to an abelian
42	variety carrying **only** the project's standard package
43	(`GrpObj`, `IsProper`, `Smooth`, `GeometricallyIrreducible`). That is the form every
44	call site has, so commutativity — and with it `MonObj.powSum` and the whole
45	symmetrisation step — is now available without threading side conditions.
46	
47	Likewise `isMonHom_of_pointed` restates Milne §I.1 Corollary 1.2 on the standard
48	package: a *pointed* morphism of abelian varieties is a homomorphism. This is the
49	`hom` input of `exists_unique_albanese_factorisation`
50	(`Albanese/AlbaneseFromData.lean`).
51	
52	## The lesson, recorded because it recurs
53	
54	The obstruction was never mathematical; it was instance **keying**. A goal stated in
55	`⊗` notation and the same goal stated in `pullback` form are definitionally equal and
56	yet only the second is solvable by synthesis. When an abelian-variety side condition
57	on `A ⊗ A` looks like missing infrastructure, try `rw [Over.tensorObj_hom]` or
58	`rw [Over.tensorObj_left]` first.
59	
60	## References
61	
62	Milne, *Abelian Varieties*, §I.1 Corollary 1.2 and Corollary 1.4. Blueprint
63	`chap:AbelianVarietyRigidity`.

80	reached by rewriting the tensor notation into pullback form. -/
81	
82	omit [IsAlgClosed kbar] in
83	/-- **The self-product of a smooth `k̄`-scheme is smooth over `k̄`.**
84	`(A ⊗ A).hom` is `pullback.fst A.hom A.hom ≫ A.hom`; the first factor is a base
85	change of the smooth `A.hom` and smoothness is stable under composition. -/
86	theorem smooth_tensorObj_self (A : Over (Spec (.of kbar))) [Smooth A.hom] :
87	    Smooth (A ⊗ A).hom := by
88	  rw [Over.tensorObj_hom]
89	  exact inferInstanceAs (Smooth (pullback.fst A.hom A.hom ≫ A.hom))
90	
91	omit [IsAlgClosed kbar] in
92	/-- **The self-product is locally of finite type over `k̄`.** Same rewrite; smooth
93	morphisms are locally of finite type and the property composes. -/
94	theorem locallyOfFiniteType_tensorObj_self (A : Over (Spec (.of kbar)))
95	    [Smooth A.hom] : LocallyOfFiniteType (A ⊗ A).hom := by
96	  rw [Over.tensorObj_hom]
97	  exact inferInstanceAs (LocallyOfFiniteType (pullback.fst A.hom A.hom ≫ A.hom))
98	
99	omit [IsAlgClosed kbar] in
100	/-- **The self-product is geometrically irreducible over `k̄`.** The projection
101	`pullback.fst A.hom A.hom` is a base change of the geometrically irreducible `A.hom`,
102	and geometric irreducibility composes (`GeometricallyIrreducible.comp`). -/
103	theorem geometricallyIrreducible_tensorObj_self (A : Over (Spec (.of kbar)))
104	    [GeometricallyIrreducible A.hom] : GeometricallyIrreducible (A ⊗ A).hom := by
105	  rw [Over.tensorObj_hom]
106	  exact GeometricallyIrreducible.comp (pullback.fst A.hom A.hom) A.hom
107	
108	/-- **The underlying scheme of the self-product is reduced.** It is smooth over `k̄`
109	by `smooth_tensorObj_self`, and a scheme smooth over an algebraically closed field is
110	reduced (`Scheme.isReduced_of_smooth_of_isAlgClosed`). -/
111	theorem isReduced_tensorObj_self_left (A : Over (Spec (.of kbar))) [Smooth A.hom] :
112	    IsReduced (A ⊗ A).left := by
113	  haveI := smooth_tensorObj_self A
114	  exact Scheme.isReduced_of_smooth_of_isAlgClosed (A ⊗ A)
115	
116	/-! ## §2. Milne I.1.2 and I.1.4 on the project's standard package
117	
118	With §1 the two rigidity corollaries apply to an abelian variety carrying only
119	`[GrpObj] [IsProper] [Smooth] [GeometricallyIrreducible]`. -/
120	
121	/-- **Milne §I.1 Corollary 1.4 on the standard package — an abelian variety is
122	commutative.**
123	
124	Same statement as `isCommMonObj_of_isProper_smooth`, but with the three self-product
125	hypotheses discharged by §1, so it applies to any `A` carrying the project's
126	four-instance abelian-variety package.
127	
128	This is what makes `MonObj.powSum` (`Albanese/GrpObjFoldSum.lean`) usable at an
129	actual abelian variety, and hence the symmetrisation step of Milne III.6.1
130	available. -/
131	theorem isCommMonObj_of_isProper_smooth_of_package (A : Over (Spec (.of kbar)))
132	    [GrpObj A] [IsProper A.hom] [Smooth A.hom] [GeometricallyIrreducible A.hom] :
133	    IsCommMonObj A := by
134	  haveI := geometricallyIrreducible_tensorObj_self A
135	  haveI := locallyOfFiniteType_tensorObj_self A
136	  haveI := isReduced_tensorObj_self_left A
137	  exact isCommMonObj_of_isProper_smooth
138	
139	/-- **Milne §I.1 Corollary 1.2 on the standard package — a pointed morphism of
140	abelian varieties is a homomorphism.**
141	
142	`av_regularMap_isHom_of_zero` with the three self-product hypotheses discharged. This
143	is exactly the `hom` input of
144	`CategoryTheory.exists_unique_albanese_factorisation`
145	(`Albanese/AlbaneseFromData.lean`): pointed rigidity for the Jacobian. -/
146	theorem isMonHom_of_pointed {A B : Over (Spec (.of kbar))}
147	    [GrpObj A] [IsProper A.hom] [Smooth A.hom] [GeometricallyIrreducible A.hom]
148	    [GrpObj B] [IsProper B.hom]
149	    (α : A ⟶ B) (hα : η[A] ≫ α = η[B]) : IsMonHom α := by
150	  haveI := geometricallyIrreducible_tensorObj_self A
151	  haveI := locallyOfFiniteType_tensorObj_self A
152	  haveI := isReduced_tensorObj_self_left A
153	  exact av_regularMap_isHom_of_zero α hα
154	
155	end AlgebraicGeometry

11	/-!
12	# The Albanese universal property of `Pic⁰_{C/k̄}`, at the Jacobian
13	
14	`Albanese/AlbaneseFromData.lean` proves Milne Proposition III.6.1 over the
15	symmetric-power interface in an arbitrary cartesian monoidal category. This file
16	instantiates it at the object the challenge cares about: `J = Pic⁰_{C/k̄}` for a
17	smooth proper geometrically irreducible curve `C` over an algebraically closed field.
18	
19	The point of the instantiation is that **every hypothesis of the general theorem is
20	discharged here except one**. Specifically:
21	
22	* `IsCommMonObj (Pic0.jacobianScheme C)` and `IsCommMonObj A` — Milne §I.1 Corollary
23	  1.4, now available on the project's four-instance package
24	  (`isCommMonObj_of_isProper_smooth_of_package`, `Albanese/AVSelfProduct.lean`).
25	* **pointed rigidity** for `Pic⁰ ⟶ A` — Milne §I.1 Corollary 1.2, likewise
26	  (`isMonHom_of_pointed`). This is the `hom` input, and it rests on the sorry-free
27	  rigidity chain of `RigidityLemma.lean`.
28	* the connector in both directions, and the assembly — proved in
29	  `Albanese/AlbaneseFromData.lean`.
30	
31	What is **not** discharged, and is the entire remaining content of this leg:
32	
33	> `SymPowData C (genus C)` — the `g`-th symmetric power of the curve, with its
34	> symmetrisation projection and universal property,
35	
36	together with the cycle map presented as the symmetrisation of a pointed Abel–Jacobi
37	map (`hf`, `haj0`) and the descent datum, which `Albanese/AlbaneseFromData.lean` §2
38	reduces to a morphism on a dense open (Milne III.5.1(a) birationality).
39	
40	## Main result
41	
42	* `Pic0.albanese_universal_property_of_symPowData` — the Albanese universal property
43	  of `Pic⁰_{C/k̄}`, with the symmetric power as an explicit argument. Axiom-clean
44	  apart from what `Pic0.jacobianScheme` itself carries (see below).
45	
46	## An honest note on `sorryAx`
47	
48	`Pic0.jacobianScheme C` is built from `Pic0.bundle`, which routes through the Picard
49	representability seam; at a *synthesis site* that seam still reports `sorryAx`
50	(the five obligations named on the AJC team thread, none of them in this leg). So this
51	theorem is **not** a closed result about the actual Jacobian, and must not be reported
52	as one. What it does establish is sharp and worth stating precisely:
53	
54	> the Albanese *argument* is complete. Given the symmetric power, Milne III.6.1 holds
55	> for `Pic⁰_{C/k̄}` with no further input from this leg.
56	
57	That is a different claim from `albanese_universal_property` in
58	`Albanese/AlbaneseUP.lean`, which quantifies over a `sorry`-bodied `abelJacobi` and a
59	`sorry`-bodied `SymmetricPower` and therefore asserts nothing about either.
60	
61	## References
62	
63	Milne, *Abelian Varieties*, §III.6 Proposition 6.1, p. 104; §I.1 Corollaries 1.2 and
64	1.4. Blueprint `thm:albanese_universal_property`.
65	-/

69	universe u
